title: Pediatric Central Diabetes Insipidus: Water Deprivation, Desmopressin and Etiologies
subject: ss-paediatric-endocrinology
module: Rickets, Calcium Disorders and Posterior Pituitary

steps.say: Excessive dilute urine output in excess of physiological norms accompanied by intense polydipsia defines polyuria.
steps.tx: Establish pathological urinary losses by checking **Classic clinical polyuria threshold in children** during initial assessment. Pathological polyuria in children is defined as urine output > 2 L/m²/day (> 4-5 mL/kg/hr in infants), accompanied by persistent intense polydipsia and craving for ice-cold water.

steps.say: Intracranial neoplasms and histiocytic infiltrates represent the most frequent identifiable organic drivers in children.
steps.tx: Investigate underlying pediatric causes by reviewing the **Etiological breakdown in children** presenting with polyuria. Pediatric central DI is caused by craniopharyngioma / germinoma (30-40%), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH, 15-20%), neurosurgical trauma, septo-optic dysplasia, or hereditary AVP mutations. Contrast neuroimaging is mandatory in all presenting cases.

vis.title: Etiological Categories of Pediatric Central DI
rows: Suprasellar mass with calcification or visual field defects
Thickened infundibulum and osteolytic bone lesions
Follows pituitary tumor resection or severe head injury
Autosomal dominant AVP-neurophysin II gene mutations

steps.say: Loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot accompanied by stalk widening signals histiocytic granulomatous infiltration.
steps.tx: Evaluate sellar and suprasellar architecture identifying **LCH pituitary stalk thickening** on contrast brain MRI. In children presenting with isolated central DI, pituitary MRI reveals thickening of the pituitary stalk (> 3 mm) and loss of the posterior pituitary T1 hyperintense bright spot, mandating staging for bone LCH.

nodes.label: Loss of Normal Posterior Pituitary T1 Bright Spot
Skeletal Survey & Staging for Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis

steps.say: Supervised fluid restriction evaluates intrinsic vasopressin release under rising plasma osmotic pressure.
steps.tx: Execute dynamic diagnostic restriction adhering to **Water deprivation protocol criteria** under strict hemodynamic monitoring. Water deprivation is halted when serum sodium reaches > 145 mEq/L or serum osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg, or if body weight drops by 3-5%; central DI fails to concentrate urine above 300 mOsm/kg.

vis.caption: Water deprivation testing curves and collecting duct aquaporin-2 channel kinetics in diabetes insipidus.

steps.say: Administration of exogenous vasopressin analog distinguishes central secretion failure from peripheral tubular resistance.
steps.tx: Differentiate central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus assessing the **Desmopressin (DDAVP) challenge test response** acutely. Subcutaneous or intranasal desmopressin (1-2 mcg SC or 10 mcg intranasal) produces a dramatic > 50% increase in urine osmolality with a prompt reduction in urine volume in central DI, but no response in nephrogenic DI.

left.title: Central DI Response
points: Prompt dramatic reduction in urine volume

right.title: Nephrogenic DI Response
points: Failure of response (< 50% rise in urine osmolality)

steps.say: Careful dose titration allows scheduled breakthrough diuresis each day to protect against water intoxication.
steps.tx: Maintain physiological fluid homeostasis by establishing **Oral and melt desmopressin titration** for outpatient therapy. Maintenance therapy uses oral desmopressin (0.05-0.2 mg TID) or sublingual melt (60-120 mcg TID), carefully titrated to permit a brief breakthrough diuresis once daily to prevent hyponatremic water intoxication.

vis.title: Desmopressin Formulations and Dosing
rows: Titrate dose allowing 1h breakthrough diuresis daily
Rapid oral transmucosal absorption unaffected by food
Variable absorption during viral rhinitis or congestion

steps.say: Hypothalamic osmoreceptor destruction eliminates the thirst mechanism and requires fixed fluid prescriptions.
steps.tx: Prevent life threatening hypernatremia by coordinating **Adipsic diabetes insipidus management** protocols after neurosurgery. Damage to hypothalamic osmoreceptors (post-craniopharyngioma resection) destroys the thirst mechanism; requires rigid daily fixed fluid prescription matched to daily morning weight to prevent severe hypernatremia. Caregivers adjust water intake dynamically based on weight shifts.

nodes.label: Daily Morning Weight & Fixed Fluid Prescription

steps.say: Neurosurgical insult to the pituitary stalk classically unfolds in a distinct three phase fluid sequence.
steps.tx: Anticipate predictable postoperative fluid transitions by monitoring the **Triphasic response after neurosurgery** closely. Pituitary surgery or head trauma triggers a classic triphasic response: Phase 1 (transient DI for 24-48h), Phase 2 (SIADH with hyponatremia at days 3-7 from dying neuron AVP leak), and Phase 3 (permanent DI after day 8).

vis.title: Triphasic Post-Neurosurgical Fluid Response
rows: Axonal shock with acute cessation of AVP secretion (polyuria)
Degenerating hypothalamic neurons leak stored AVP (hyponatremia)
Irreversible neuronal death with permanent loss of AVP
